paragraphs: A prediction interval is useful only if its stated confidence matches how often it actually covers the outcome. Bayesian methods provide uncertainty estimates, but imperfect models and approximate inference can make those estimates misleading. For example, an interval labeled 90% may cover the true outcome less or more often than that label suggests.

The paper proposes a simple calibration procedure for regression algorithms. It extends an idea associated with Platt scaling in classification to predictions of numerical outcomes. Applied to Bayesian and other probabilistic models, the procedure has a guarantee of calibrated uncertainty when enough data are available. That data requirement is part of the claim, rather than an unconditional promise about every fitted model.

The authors evaluate the procedure with Bayesian linear regression and feedforward and recurrent neural networks. They report consistently well-calibrated credible intervals and improved performance in time series forecasting and model-based reinforcement learning. These findings connect better uncertainty estimates to practical prediction and decision tasks, beyond merely changing the confidence labels attached to predictions.
icml-2018-accurate-uncertainties-for-dee.tldr: A regression calibration procedure makes uncertainty estimates reliable given enough data and improves performance in the evaluated forecasting and reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent uses noisy gradient information, yet it can work remarkably well on neural network objectives with complicated geometry. This paper studies that behavior by viewing SGD as operating on a smoothed version of the loss. The relevant landscape is therefore shaped by averages over neighborhoods, rather than solely by the gradient at an individual point.

The main guarantee requires a particular condition: at every point, a weighted average of nearby gradients must satisfy one-point convexity relative to the desired solution. Under that condition, SGD approaches the solution and then remains nearby with constant probability. The original objective may still contain many poor local minima or saddle points, so the result covers a substantially broader class than convex functions.

The authors also observe favorable local one-point convexity properties in neural network loss surfaces. This empirical finding helps connect their theorem to neural network training. It supports an explanation for SGD's effectiveness, while preserving the distinction between locally observed geometry and the theorem's condition across every point.
icml-2018-an-alternative-view-when-does-.tldr: Viewing SGD through a smoothed loss yields a conditional guarantee that it can approach and remain near a desired solution despite bad local minima.

paragraphs: The Rasch model supports analysis of responses to items in settings such as tests, surveys, and recommendation systems. Estimating its parameters is a longstanding problem, but many existing performance guarantees describe behavior only as the amount of data becomes very large. Such guarantees offer less direct guidance when deciding how large a particular study should be.

This paper introduces a framework built around a linear minimum mean-squared error estimator. Its central contribution is an exact, closed-form analysis of parameter estimation error that applies without taking an asymptotic limit. That makes estimation accuracy something the framework can characterize for finite amounts of data under the Rasch model.

The analysis provides guidance on how many items and responses are needed to obtain low estimation error in tests or surveys. The authors also evaluate the estimator on real collaborative filtering datasets, where its predictive performance matches that of leading nonlinear estimators. The result combines analytical tractability with competitive prediction in those evaluations.
icml-2018-an-estimation-and-analysis-fra.tldr: A linear Rasch-model estimator enables exact finite-data error analysis and matches leading nonlinear estimators on evaluated collaborative filtering datasets.

paragraphs: Building a decision tree requires choosing how to split examples at each step. Measures such as entropy and Gini impurity assess how mixed the resulting groups are. For a categorical attribute with many possible values, deciding which values belong on each side of a binary split creates a difficult search problem.

Practical tree-building methods commonly use heuristics to find low-impurity splits in this setting. The paper identifies a gap in that approach: the quality of those heuristic choices lacks known guarantees. It introduces two splitting procedures with proofs that their impurity is near optimal, giving a principled quality guarantee for this individual decision within tree construction.

The authors also report experiments supporting the procedures as promising choices for categorical attributes with many values in decision trees and random forests. The theoretical result concerns the quality of the splits themselves. The experimental evidence motivates using those procedures during induction without claiming that every resulting tree or forest must achieve superior predictive performance.
icml-2018-binary-partitions-with-approxi.tldr: Two decision-tree splitting procedures provide near-optimal impurity guarantees for categorical attributes with many values.

paragraphs: Online optimization repeatedly selects a decision while trying to keep average cost low over time. When valid decisions must satisfy combinatorial constraints, even the operations needed to make each choice can become computationally difficult. The paper addresses that obstacle by changing how the set of permissible decisions is represented.

Its approach first compiles Boolean constraints into a deterministic and decomposable negation normal form circuit, abbreviated dDNNF. Once constraints have this representation, linear optimization and sampling valid solutions take time linear in the circuit size. This shifts attention from repeatedly handling raw constraints to performing efficient operations on a compiled representation.

Using this framework, the authors give efficient formulations of existing combinatorial prediction strategies, with particular emphasis on mirror descent. They compare those strategies on real-world benchmarks whose constraints are compiled beforehand. The distinction between preliminary compilation and subsequent operations matters: the stated linear-time benefits apply to operations on the circuit, rather than establishing that arbitrary constraint systems are easy to compile.
icml-2018-compiling-combinatorial-predic.tldr: Compiling combinatorial constraints into dDNNF circuits enables efficient optimization and sampling for online prediction strategies.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing methods often estimate worker reliability using simplified models of mistakes. In the setting described here, conventional assumptions make workers' errors independent of one another and give each worker the same error probability across tasks. These restrictions exclude coordinated behavior and workers whose reliability changes with the task.

The paper studies a substantially more permissive setting. Almost half of the workers may depart from the one-coin model, with task-dependent error probabilities and arbitrary correlations among their mistakes. Those workers can even collude perfectly. Adversarial behavior therefore includes coordinated answers, rather than merely individual workers who happen to be inaccurate.

Within this setting, the authors design an efficient algorithm that consistently estimates workers' error probabilities. Consistency means the estimates approach their targets as the available evidence grows. The contribution is a reliability-estimation guarantee despite a large, potentially coordinated adversarial group. The fraction matters: the stated model allows almost half of the workers to deviate, rather than placing no restriction on how many workers behave adversarially.
icml-2018-crowdsourcing-with-arbitrary-a.tldr: An efficient crowdsourcing algorithm consistently estimates worker error probabilities even when almost half the workers can behave adversarially and collude.

paragraphs: Algorithmic stability links how sensitive training is to its data with how well the learned model generalizes. Previous stability analyses of stochastic gradient descent used distribution-free, worst-case quantities. This paper develops a data-dependent notion of stability, allowing the resulting generalization bounds to reflect properties of the learning problem more directly.

The analysis highlights initialization in two different settings. For convex objectives, the bound on generalization error depends on the risk at the starting point. For nonconvex objectives, the expected curvature near that point has an important influence. These results connect generalization to where optimization begins, as well as to properties of the objective encountered there.

Both findings suggest screening candidate initializations using data as a way to stabilize SGD. The paper also derives optimistic bounds with fast convergence rates when empirical risk vanishes and stochastic gradient noise is low. Those conditions are essential to that favorable conclusion; the work does not assert that every SGD run automatically receives the same fast generalization rate.
icml-2018-data-dependent-stability-of-st.tldr: Data-dependent stability bounds connect SGD generalization to initialization and yield fast rates under vanishing empirical risk and low gradient noise.

paragraphs: A deep linear network stacks linear transformations, creating a layered parameterization even though the resulting input-output mapping remains linear. This paper examines whether that parameterization can introduce local minima with worse objective values than the best possible solution. The analysis applies to loss functions that are both convex and differentiable.

The authors give a short, elementary proof that every local minimum is global under either of two width conditions. All hidden layers may be at least as wide as the input layer, or they may all be at least as wide as the output layer. Under these assumptions, a locally optimal set of network parameters cannot have a suboptimal loss value.

The paper also establishes why differentiability matters. If the loss remains convex and Lipschitz but is no longer differentiable, suboptimal local minima can occur. This counterpoint defines the stated sense in which the result is strongest possible. The guarantee concerns the structure of local minima under the given assumptions, rather than an asserted convergence rate for a training algorithm.
icml-2018-deep-linear-networks-with-arbi.tldr: For convex differentiable losses and specified hidden-layer widths, every local minimum of a deep linear network is global.

paragraphs: Sequence data can contain patterns that recur within the recent history. A model that adapts as it processes a sequence can use those repetitions to revise its predictions. This paper explores dynamic evaluation, in which gradient descent updates the sequence model using recently observed material, increasing the probability it assigns to recurring patterns.

The authors develop an adaptation approach that outperforms the existing adaptation methods included in their comparisons. The central idea is to make recent sequence history influence the model through parameter updates. Evaluation therefore includes ongoing learning from that history, allowing the predictor to respond to patterns in the sequence currently being processed.

The reported results improve on previous word-level perplexities on Penn Treebank and WikiText-2, reaching 51.1 and 44.3. They also improve on previous character-level cross-entropies on text8 and the Hutter Prize datasets, reaching 1.19 and 1.08 bits per character. These findings demonstrate the value of dynamic adaptation across both word and character prediction in the evaluated datasets.
icml-2018-dynamic-evaluation-of-neural-s.tldr: Updating sequence models from recent history improves prediction of recurring patterns and achieves leading reported word- and character-level results.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained convolutional network assumes that some features learned on the source task will also help with the target task. This is especially useful when target data are limited and learning those features from scratch would be difficult. However, starting from pretrained parameters does not by itself explicitly encourage retaining them throughout adaptation.

The paper investigates regularization schemes that favor final models similar to the pretrained model. Such penalties make the preference for preserving source-task knowledge part of the optimization objective. They supplement the influence already provided by initialization and early stopping, giving fine-tuning an explicit bias toward its starting solution.

The authors report benefits from this approach and recommend a simple L2 penalty measured relative to the pretrained parameters as a baseline for transfer learning. In plain terms, adaptation is allowed, but moving away from the initial model carries a cost. The recommendation makes the useful prior model a continuing reference during training, rather than only the place where training begins.
icml-2018-explicit-inductive-bias-for-tr.tldr: Regularizing fine-tuned networks toward their pretrained parameters provides a useful explicit bias for transfer learning.

paragraphs: Optimization methods can be studied as dynamical systems whose states move toward better solutions over time. This viewpoint brings tools from differential equations and control theory to the design of fast algorithms. The paper develops a class of hybrid control systems with continuous evolution governed by a second-order differential equation.

The distinctive component is damping that depends on the current state but has no explicit time dependence. It acts as a feedback control input, adjusting the system's evolution according to where it is. For a user-chosen scalar alpha, the authors prove convergence to a global optimizer at a rate of order exp(-alpha t), provided the objective satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality.

That objective condition is central to the guarantee. The paper also introduces a discretization whose resulting discrete dynamical system retains exponential convergence. This connects the continuous-time analysis to a step-by-step system, showing that the framework's fast convergence is not confined to the differential equation alone.
icml-2018-fast-gradient-based-methods-wi.tldr: State-dependent damping yields exponential convergence in a hybrid optimization framework for objectives satisfying the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality.

paragraphs: Optimization on the integer lattice chooses integer-valued quantities rather than only deciding whether individual elements are included. Many studied methods rely on submodularity, a form of diminishing returns. The paper addresses monotonic objectives that need not have that property, broadening the optimization setting to accommodate applications outside the usual submodular framework.

The authors provide two approximation algorithms for maximizing such objectives under a cardinality constraint, which limits the total amount selected. They identify these as the first algorithms for this purpose with polynomial query complexity. This guarantee concerns how many queries the algorithms make to the objective, while the solutions they return are approximate rather than asserted to be exact optima.

The paper also introduces an integer-lattice framework for influence maximization that generalizes earlier work. Within that application, the authors demonstrate the efficiency of their algorithms. The contribution thus combines algorithmic guarantees with an application framework, showing how optimization beyond submodularity can support a broader formulation of influence allocation.
icml-2018-fast-maximization-of-non-submo.tldr: Two approximation algorithms achieve polynomial query complexity for cardinality-constrained maximization of non-submodular monotonic integer-lattice objectives.

paragraphs: Compositional understanding means using familiar pieces in new combinations according to their meanings. Learning a new action should, for example, make it possible to understand instructions that repeat or combine that action. This paper investigates whether sequence-to-sequence recurrent networks generalize in this systematic way, rather than merely succeeding on unfamiliar but closely related sequences.

The authors introduce SCAN, a domain pairing simple navigation commands with action sequences. They train several recurrent networks and test their ability to handle commands absent from training. The networks succeed when training and test commands differ only modestly, allowing combinations of familiar patterns, but fail severely when the tests demand systematic compositional skills.

These results distinguish successful zero-shot prediction from the stronger ability to apply learned meanings consistently across new contexts. A further proof-of-concept experiment in neural machine translation suggests that limited systematicity may partly explain neural networks' demand for large training datasets. That broader explanation is presented as a possibility supported by the experiment, rather than a universal conclusion.
icml-2018-generalization-without-systema.tldr: SCAN experiments show that tested recurrent sequence models can generalize to nearby combinations while failing at systematic composition.

paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-learning uses multiple tasks to learn shared structure that can help a model adapt to a new task. The paper observes that earlier methods still use simple gradient descent during that adaptation. MT-net expands what is learned across tasks by shaping both the space available for adaptation and the geometry of the updates.

For each layer's activations, the meta-learner selects a subspace in which the task-specific learner performs gradient descent. It also learns a distance metric that changes how movement through activation space is measured. This reshaping makes the space more sensitive to task identity, so adaptation follows structure learned from the collection of tasks.

The authors demonstrate that the learned subspace's dimension reflects the complexity of the adaptation problem. They also find less sensitivity to initial learning-rate choices than in earlier gradient-based meta-learning methods. On few-shot classification and regression tasks, MT-net achieves leading or comparable performance, supporting the usefulness of learning how adaptation should proceed as well as shared task information.
icml-2018-gradient-based-meta-learning-w.tldr: MT-net learns layerwise adaptation subspaces and distance metrics, achieving competitive few-shot performance with reduced learning-rate sensitivity.

paragraphs: Learning a long sequence of decisions is difficult when useful rewards occur only rarely. An agent may spend substantial effort exploring before receiving evidence that its behavior is promising. Expert guidance can help, but obtaining that guidance also has a cost. This paper studies how to use expert feedback effectively in such settings.

The proposed framework, hierarchical guidance, uses the problem's hierarchical structure to combine different forms of expert interaction. Imitation learning and reinforcement learning can be assigned in different combinations at different levels. This provides a way to distribute learning and guidance across the hierarchy, with the aim of reducing both expert effort and exploration cost.

On long-horizon benchmarks, including Montezuma's Revenge, the authors demonstrate significantly faster learning than hierarchical reinforcement learning and significantly greater label efficiency than standard imitation learning. They also analyze labeling cost theoretically for certain versions of the framework. The theoretical scope is therefore tied to those instantiations, while the benchmark results provide empirical support for the broader approach.
icml-2018-hierarchical-imitation-and-rei.tldr: Hierarchical guidance combines imitation and reinforcement learning across levels to reduce expert labeling and exploration effort on long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: A GAN's discriminator usually judges generated examples individually. That limits its access to statistics describing a collection of generated samples, which can contribute to mode dropping: the generator represents only part of the target distribution. This paper changes the discriminator's task so that it receives information about batches as a whole.

The proposed discriminator takes a mixture of real and generated examples and predicts the fraction that is real. Because this fraction does not depend on sample order, the authors build permutation invariance directly into the architecture. They prove that the architecture can universally approximate symmetric functions, giving it broad representational capacity for functions whose outputs ignore ordering.

Experiments show reduced mode collapse on two synthetic datasets and good qualitative and quantitative results on CIFAR10 and CelebA. These findings support batch-level feedback as a way to address missing distributional diversity. The approximation theorem concerns what the discriminator architecture can represent; the reduction in collapse is established empirically in the reported experiments.
icml-2018-mixed-batches-and-symmetric-di.tldr: A permutation-invariant discriminator predicts the real-sample fraction in mixed batches and empirically reduces GAN mode collapse.

paragraphs: Complex collective behavior can arise from interactions among relatively simple components. Understanding such a system requires learning both how its components behave and which components influence one another. Neural relational inference addresses these two tasks together, using observational data without supervised labels for the underlying interaction structure.

The model is a variational autoencoder whose hidden representation is an interaction graph. A graph neural network uses that representation to reconstruct the observed dynamics. This connects the inferred relationships to their ability to explain the system's behavior, so learning the graph and learning the dynamics become parts of the same modeling process.

In simulated physical systems, the authors show that the model can accurately recover the known interactions without supervision. On motion capture and sports tracking data, they report interpretable structure and prediction of complex dynamics. The simulations support comparison with ground-truth relationships, while the real-data results demonstrate that the approach can produce understandable relational descriptions alongside useful predictions.
icml-2018-neural-relational-inference-fo.tldr: Neural relational inference jointly learns interaction graphs and system dynamics from observations without supervised interaction labels.

paragraphs: The paper formulates regression fairness in terms of association between predictions and sensitive attributes, such as race, gender, or age. For multiple sensitive attributes, it uses the coefficient of determination as an extension of correlation. This gives a specific measurable fairness criterion with which to express a user's desired constraint.

Rather than requiring perfect fairness regardless of predictive usefulness, the method optimizes accuracy subject to a chosen fairness level. That constraint makes the feasible region nonconvex, preventing direct use of an ordinary convex optimizer. The authors nevertheless show that tools from global optimization yield an exact solution to the problem they formulate.

The paper also extends the method to nonlinear prediction through a kernel representation. It supports numerical sensitive attributes and multiple sensitive attributes, expanding the types of fairness constraints that can be handled. Its contribution is a tractable treatment of the accuracy–fairness trade-off under the stated association-based criterion, with an exact optimization result despite the constraint's nonconvexity.
icml-2018-nonconvex-optimization-for-reg.tldr: Global optimization yields an exact regression solution under a user-chosen correlation-based fairness constraint, with a kernel extension for nonlinear prediction.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of the network's output. Convolutional networks use this principle for translations, and researchers have sought related constructions for graphs, manifolds, and other domains. This paper provides a rigorous account of convolution and equivariance for actions of compact groups.

Its main theorem establishes a two-way relationship under stated natural constraints. Convolutional structure is sufficient to obtain equivariance, but it is also necessary within that setting. This makes convolution more than one available architectural choice: the symmetry requirement itself imposes convolutional structure when the theorem's constraints apply.

The authors develop the argument using representation theory and noncommutative harmonic analysis, and derive new generalized convolution formulas. These tools give a mathematical basis for extending symmetry-aware neural networks beyond familiar translation-based constructions. The qualification on the theorem matters: the necessity result holds within its constrained setting, rather than asserting that every conceivable equivariant architecture must have the same structure.
icml-2018-on-the-generalization-of-equiv.tldr: Under natural constraints, convolutional structure is both necessary and sufficient for neural-network equivariance to compact-group actions.

paragraphs: Weighted correlation clustering poses difficult optimization and approximation problems on general graphs, despite its usefulness in network analysis and computer vision. This paper develops three complementary tools: conditions for establishing parts of an optimal solution, fast lower bounds, and a way to improve solutions found through local search.

The partial optimality conditions can be checked efficiently. Applying them recursively solves series-parallel graphs exactly in linear time, giving a strong result for that graph class. For more general instances, the authors use a packing dual formulation to obtain a nontrivial lower bound through a heuristic procedure that runs faster than a canonical linear programming relaxation.

A third contribution uses the dual solution to reweight the problem so that efficient local search algorithms converge to better feasible solutions. Benchmark experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods. The contributions serve different purposes: partial optimality certifies structure, lower bounds help assess achievable cost, and reweighting improves search, without claiming an efficient exact solution for arbitrary graphs.
icml-2018-partial-optimality-and-fast-lo.tldr: Partial optimality tests, fast lower bounds, and dual-based reweighting improve weighted correlation clustering, with exact linear-time solutions for series-parallel graphs.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learns which action to choose from the rewards it observes. This paper considers rewards with two components: a linear function of known action features and an additional nonlinear term that does not depend on the action. The latter can complicate learning even though it is shared across actions.

The authors design algorithms with regret bounded by roughly d times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, for d-dimensional linear features over T rounds. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to better action choices. The bound matches the best known rate for the simpler setting without this confounding term and improves on the prior result identified in the abstract.

The algorithms use a new reward estimator inspired by doubly robust methods, supported by new concentration inequalities for self-normalized martingales. Empirical evaluations show better performance than prior approaches when rewards contain nonlinear confounding effects. Together, the theory and experiments show that the stated action-independent confounding structure can be handled without worsening the best known regret order.
icml-2018-semiparametric-contextual-band.tldr: New contextual-bandit algorithms handle nonlinear action-independent confounding while matching the best known regret order for unconfounded linear bandits.

paragraphs: A changing process requires a predictor to recognize when previously useful patterns stop applying. When observations also interact across space, detecting those changes involves more than tracking a single time series. This paper extends Bayesian online changepoint detection to nonstationary spatio-temporal processes while also selecting models as observations arrive.

Between changepoints, the proposed method represents the process with spatially structured vector autoregressions. These models use relationships across variables and time to describe behavior within a segment. The authors provide an upper bound on their approximation error, giving theoretical support for this modeling choice alongside the change-detection procedure.

The resulting algorithm performs prediction, model selection, and changepoint detection online. The abstract reports linear time complexity and constant space complexity, together with a speed advantage of two orders of magnitude over the closest competitor. It also reports improved performance over the state of the art for multivariate data. The contribution brings these three ongoing inference tasks into one computationally efficient framework.
icml-2018-spatio-temporal-bayesian-on-li.tldr: An online Bayesian framework combines prediction, model selection, and changepoint detection for changing spatio-temporal data with reported speed and performance gains.

paragraphs: This paper studies the geometry of neural network losses when the network uses ReLU or leaky ReLU activations and a hinge loss criterion. In parameter space, the resulting loss has a piecewise multilinear structure. That algebraic structure provides a route to understanding where local minima can occur.

Using harmonic analysis, the authors show that every local minimum is nondifferentiable unless it lies in a region where the loss is perfectly flat. Consequently, the points at which ordinary derivatives fail are central to the optimization landscape in this setting. Treating them merely as exceptional technical complications would miss the locations of the nonflat local minima.

The result motivates using nonsmooth analysis to study these networks, and the paper demonstrates such techniques in illustrative cases. Its main contribution is a structural characterization that directs attention toward the appropriate mathematical tools. The finding is tied to the stated activations and hinge loss, and distinguishes nondifferentiable minima from the special case of minima within flat regions.
icml-2018-the-multilinear-structure-of-r.tldr: For hinge-loss ReLU and leaky ReLU networks, local minima are nondifferentiable unless they occur in perfectly flat loss regions.

paragraphs: A calibrated classifier's confidence should agree with how often its predictions are correct. Neural networks can be overconfident, but reducing confidence across the board also weakens predictions that deserve high confidence. This paper instead proposes directly minimizing a measure of calibration error during network training.

The measure, MMCE, uses a kernel construction in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. It can be trained efficiently alongside the negative likelihood loss without careful hyperparameter tuning. The authors establish that it is minimized at perfect calibration and that its finite-sample estimates are consistent with fast convergence rates, connecting the training objective to a theoretically supported calibration criterion.

Experiments across several network architectures show that MMCE reduces calibration error quickly and stably while preserving high-confidence predictions. The approach therefore targets the mismatch between confidence and correctness more specifically than methods that simply suppress confidence. Its theoretical properties concern the calibration measure and its estimation, while the reported experiments establish the practical behavior of training networks with it.
icml-2018-trainable-calibration-measures.tldr: MMCE adds a theoretically grounded calibration objective to neural-network training, reducing calibration error while preserving high-confidence predictions.

paragraphs: One explanation for successful neural network training is that local minima may all produce similarly good results. This paper examines a precise version of that idea for binary classification. It focuses on training error, separating the ability to classify the training examples correctly from performance on new examples.

The authors give conditions under which every local minimum of an appropriately chosen surrogate loss has zero training error. Roughly, neurons must be increasing and strictly convex; the architecture must be single-layered or include a shortcut-like connection when multilayered; and training must use a smooth hinge-like surrogate loss. The guarantee depends on this combination of activation, architecture, and objective conditions.

Counterexamples show that relaxing those conditions can make the result fail. This establishes a meaningful boundary around the positive theorem, rather than treating good local minima as a universal feature of neural networks. The finding explains when local optimality can certify perfect training classification in the studied setting, without extending that certificate to generalization performance.
icml-2018-understanding-the-loss-surface.tldr: Under specified activation, architecture, and surrogate-loss conditions, every local minimum has zero binary-classification training error.
